passage: The storm over Bengaluru had cancelled every evening flight, and Rukmini sat at the gate with a dead phone battery and a sinking stomach. Rukmini's father, in Kolkata, had a hospital appointment on Monday and had insisted, over the phone, "Don't come just for that, you have your work." Rukmini felt the familiar guilt: for living so far away, for missing birthdays, for this too. But sitting there, the guilt did something useful. Rukmini borrowed a charger from the woman next to the seat, called Aparna, a cousin near the father's house, and asked her to go along on Monday. Then Rukmini booked a cab for the father and, at last, a ticket for the weekend after. "I'll come properly," Rukmini said on the call. "Three days, no laptop."

qa.q: What was Rukmini feeling at the gate, and what did the feeling do?
qa.a: Guilt about living far away, missing birthdays and now this appointment, and it pushed Rukmini toward practical steps instead of just tormenting.

qa.q: What practical steps did Rukmini take?
qa.a: Rukmini asked the cousin Aparna to go with the father on Monday, booked a cab for him and booked a ticket for the following weekend for a proper visit.

qa.q: How might Rukmini's father have felt about the situation?
qa.a: He was trying not to be a burden, as "Don't come just for that, you have your work" suggests, and probably was reassured by Aparna going with him.

grounding: Shows living far from parents for work and feeling guilty, staying in contact, arranging practical support and planning an honest visit so that guilt moves action.

passage:
Parveen, you think you are the first child to live far from her parents? Sit. Your Samir chacha has a story.

At twenty-four I got a job in Muscat. Ammi and Abbu stayed in Lucknow. The first year, I sent money and felt guilty every day. Every festival photo from home was a knife. I would lie awake calculating how old Abbu was, and do nothing except feel terrible.

Then Ammi fell in the courtyard and a neighbour found her. That woke me up. Guilt that only hurts is useless, beta. So I changed things. I called every Sunday at nine, same time, so they could wait for it. I paid a boy from the lane to bring vegetables and check on them daily. I came home every Eid, and when I came, I switched off my phone.

I still missed them. But I stopped drowning in it and started doing something.

qa.q: Where did young Samir work, and where did his parents live?
qa.a: He worked in Muscat, and his parents stayed in Lucknow.

qa.q: How did young Samir feel during his first year away?
qa.a: He felt guilty every day, lying awake and feeling terrible without doing anything about it.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Samir's story?
qa.a: His mother's fall in the courtyard made him turn guilt into action: regular Sunday calls, a boy to check on them daily, and full attention on Eid visits.

qa.q: How might Ammi and Abbu have felt once the Sunday calls began?
qa.a: They probably felt comforted and looked forward to the fixed time, knowing their son would call.

grounding: An elder's story shows a young man living far from his parents for work, whose guilt first torments him and then moves him to regular contact, practical support and real visits.

passage:
The rain had cut the railway line to Siliguri, and Sudha's leave application had been rejected that morning. In her Bengaluru PG, she watched her mother on a video call trying to stand up from the sofa after the fall. It took three tries.

"Don't come, Sudha, the trains aren't even running," Ma said. Sudha felt sick with guilt. Everyone else's daughter lived nearby.

She let herself cry for ten minutes. Then she opened a notebook. She called Shreya, the neighbours' daughter, who worked from home. "Could you look in on Ma each evening? I'll pay for anything she needs." Shreya said yes at once. Sudha ordered groceries to be delivered, set a daily nine o'clock video call, and spoke to her manager about working from Siliguri for two weeks next month.

That night Ma said, "You're far, but you're here." Sudha slept, for the first time in two days.

qa.q: What had cut the railway line to Siliguri?
qa.a: The rain had cut the railway line.

qa.q: What was Sudha feeling as she watched her mother try to stand?
qa.a: Sudha felt sick with guilt at being far away while her mother struggled.

qa.q: How did Sudha use her guilt well?
qa.a: After a short cry she made a plan: a neighbour to check in, groceries delivered, a fixed daily call and a request to work from Siliguri.

qa.q: What is it like for Sudha's mother after the plan is in place?
qa.a: She feels cared for despite the distance, saying, "You're far, but you're here."

grounding: The story shows a young woman living far from her parent for work, whose guilt moves her to arrange practical support, regular contact and an honest visit.
